Hatchlings are surprisingly small given the adult dimensions of this species, with a carapace length at birth of just 5.28 cm [Lb = 5.28 cm] and a corresponding wet weight at birth of 31.2 grams [Wwb = 31.2 grams]. This initial mass is modest compared to the range reported in some field studies, where values between 34 and 70 grams have occasionally been noted, suggesting considerable variation in yolk provisioning among clutches. The relatively diminutive size of neonates is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes prolonged survivorship and eventual large adult body size over rapid early growth. Upon emergence, the young turtles are immediately capable of aquatic locomotion and begin seeking cover in submerged vegetation, relying on residual yolk reserves for the first several days before commencing exogenous feeding.

Juvenile Dermatemys mawii exhibit a rapid growth phase during the initial twelve months following birth, with individuals reaching a carapace length of 14.7 cm  and a wet weight of 475 grams  by the end of their first year. This represents a near-tripling of their birth length and a more than fifteenfold increase in body mass, reflecting the high productivity of the lowland riverine habitats they occupy. Growth trajectories show that a turtle measuring 30 cm in carapace length will attain a length of 34 cm  over the subsequent three years, with a corresponding increase in wet weight from approximately 800 grams to 2300 grams . This deceleration in relative growth rate as size increases is a common pattern among large-bodied freshwater turtles, where energetic demands for somatic expansion eventually compete with the onset of reproductive investment. Field recapture data from Belizean populations confirm that juvenile survivorship remains high throughout this period, likely due to the absence of significant aquatic predators in their deep-water refuges. Continued growth under favorable conditions leads to a further expansion, with individuals reaching 38 cm  in carapace length within another three-year interval after their mass has crossed 3200 grams; the corresponding wet weight at this stage climbs to 6000 grams . Ultimately, a turtle that has attained 42 cm  in carapace length will weigh approximately 8400 grams  after three additional years of growth from the 5200-gram benchmark.

Sexual maturation in Dermatemys mawii is closely tied to body size rather than chronological age alone, with females attaining puberty at a carapace length of 41 cm [Lp = 41 cm] and a wet weight of 10600 grams [Wwp = 10600 grams], whereas males become reproductively mature at a smaller carapace length of 37.5 cm [Lp = 37.5 cm] and a wet weight of 9600 grams [Wwp = 9600 grams]. This size dimorphism at maturation is typical of many emydid and geoemydid turtles, though it is less pronounced in this species than in some of its kin. Field studies indicate that females generally begin ovipositing between 39.5 and 42.0 cm, while males initiate spermatogenesis between 36.5 and 38.5 cm, confirming the narrow but consistent threshold for reproductive activation. The time since birth at puberty for animals maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] is estimated at approximately 7 years [tp = approximately 7 years], though this figure is derived from growth curves and may vary with resource availability and local thermal regimes. Following puberty, individuals continue to grow at a reduced rate, ultimately approaching the asymptotic dimensions of the species, with a maximum recorded carapace length of 65 cm [Li = 65 cm] and an ultimate wet weight of 22000 grams [Wwi = 22000 grams], making Dermatemys mawii one of the largest entirely aquatic freshwater turtles in the Neotropics.

The leathery-shelled eggs are deposited in shallow nests excavated along sandy banks, where they undergo a prolonged incubation period that is highly sensitive to thermal fluctuations. Gravid females typically move only short distances from their aquatic home ranges to oviposit, a behavior that minimizes terrestrial exposure to potential predators.

The maximum lifespan documented for Dermatemys mawii in captivity, under thermal conditions averaging 28 °C [T = 28 °C], is approximately 11.3 years [am = approximately 11.3 years], though it is widely suspected that wild individuals may exceed this figure, given the species' slow somatic growth and late maturation. This longevity, while not extreme among turtles, is notable for a species that occupies a relatively seasonal and productive environment, where the trade-off between rapid growth and extended survivorship appears to favor the latter. Comparisons with other members of the Dermatemydidae are limited because the family is monotypic, but among large emydids of similar adult mass, lifespans of 15 to 25 years are common, suggesting that the captive record for D. mawii may underestimate true potential. The physiological mechanisms underlying this species' longevity are poorly understood, though its low resting metabolic rate and efficient nitrogen excretion likely contribute to reduced oxidative stress over time. Senescence in wild populations has not been systematically studied, but the presence of very large, scarred individuals in museum collections indicates that some animals attain substantial ages. Given the ongoing threats from habitat destruction and overharvesting for local consumption, understanding the full lifespan and reproductive window of this critically endangered species remains a priority for effective conservation planning.
